trans-unit.source: Your cluster on every screen, and in every terminal

The web console is the center. Around it: a code-signed desktop app with its own VPN tunnel, mobile apps for alerts and approvals on the go, a CLI for scripts and pipelines, and an MCP server for your agents.
Request early access
Remote access
Loadweaver Desktop
The console as a native app, with the fleet view, OS notifications for alerts, and terminals and tunnels one click away. It runs your VPN tunnel too.
OS-native WireGuard
Kernel WireGuard on Linux, wireguard-nt on Windows and WireGuardKit in a Network Extension on macOS. No own crypto.
Enrollment and posture
Enrollment, key renewal after sign-in and posture reports, plus a view of the services you may reach.
Code-signed
Apple Developer ID with notarization, Windows Authenticode, and signed apt and rpm repositories on Linux, with checksums on top.
Verified updates
In-app updates on stable and beta channels, verified by signature and manifest before install, and never silently downgraded.
Loadweaver Desktop with a connected tunnel through gateway gw1, company sign-in, a device key that renews after sign-in, passed posture checks and the internal services the user's policies allow.
Loadweaver for phones and tablets
The console in a mobile layout: the overview and the needs-attention inbox, alerts as push notifications, approvals on the go, logs and the map.
Available in the App Store and Google Play, and through managed distribution with Intune, Jamf or Kandji.
Alerts and approvals
Push notifications when something needs attention, and approvals for plans wherever you are.
A tunnel in your pocket
WireGuardKit in a Packet Tunnel extension on iOS and the official wireguard-android library on Android.
Posture you can trust
Passcode or biometrics, OS patch level, jailbreak and root detection, and app attestation so reports cannot be faked by a modified app.
A CLI for people, an MCP server for agents
Both work against the same API as the console, with the same access rules, approvals and audit trail.

A Loadweaver plan in the terminal: a new deployment, a changed policy that adds a WireGuard peer and a route, a DNS record and a certificate, followed by the failure analysis with one unacknowledged pin.
Loadweaver CLI

Single binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64. Published on npm, GitHub releases, an install script, Homebrew, a deb / rpm repository and as a container image, signed with cosign and checksums.
MCP server

loadweaver mcp in the CLI for local agents, and a remote MCP endpoint for hosted agents, including Agenstra's. Agents can read state, query logs and metrics, create plans and request approvals, but never bypass them.

Compare with self-hosted

Loadweaver topology map: two sites with five nodes, encrypted WireGuard tunnels between the sites, a failover IP on an ingress node with a standby at the other site, a volume replicated synchronously within a site and asynchronously across sites, and live traffic from the internet.
The same product, without running it yourself
Loadweaver Cloud is not a shared platform. Each customer gets a cluster of their own, and it is a full Loadweaver cluster from the first node.
Your own control plane
Control plane, nodes and keys belong to your cluster alone.
Ready from day one
The first node already runs the control plane and the console, so your cluster is complete before the second node joins.
Grows like any cluster
Add nodes and sites whenever you need them, through plan and apply, bounded by your quotas.
More nodes, on your provider accounts
Your cluster orders further nodes itself, through plan and apply, with the provider tokens you configure in it.
Your provider account
Hetzner Cloud, DigitalOcean or another provider plugin, with your token
Your Loadweaver cluster
Orders the node through plan and apply, within your quotas
A new node
Joins the cluster, and is drained before it is ever deleted
Your own keys
Add your provider accounts to the cluster, or hand over the tokens when you order. With your own keys you pay the provider directly.
Kept as secrets
Tokens end up as Loadweaver secrets and are never shown in plans, logs or the audit trail.
Provider plugins
Hetzner Cloud and DigitalOcean out of the box, and more providers through dynamic provider plugins.
Leaving is data-safe too
Removing a node or cancelling the subscription follows the same rule as everything else: nothing is lost without your choice.
Final backup
Before teardown, a final backup goes to your external backup target, if you configured one.
Read-only grace period
You keep read-only access for export during a grace period.
Only what we deployed

We delete the server we provisioned, its IPs and DNS records. Nodes in your own provider accounts are not deleted; Loadweaver offers to decommission them or leaves them for re-use. Every step is audited.

Kubernetes is the industry standard for container orchestration, with a large ecosystem of add-ons for networking, storage and observability. k3s packages it as a lightweight distribution for small clusters and the edge. It fits when you want the Kubernetes API and ecosystem and have the know-how to operate it.

Resilient clusters from a handful of servers

Loadweaver turns a handful of servers into a resilient multi-site cluster. It gives applications built with AI, and the agents behind them, a protected home on infrastructure you control, with encrypted traffic between sites and services that keep running when a location goes down.
Bring the Docker Compose files you already have. Every change is a plan you review before it is applied, and no single server failure takes an app down.

High availability for the servers you already have

Loadweaver starts where small fleets are: a handful of nodes, often spread across sites. You get a cluster that survives the loss of a server, without the overhead of running Kubernetes, and it grows with you to around 1,000 nodes per cluster.
Start with one node, grow when you need to

A single node is already a complete setup. Nodes can join and leave over and over again: growing from one to many and shrinking back is a normal operation, not a migration project. When a node leaves, it is drained first, and nothing is dropped without your choice.
One node to start. More sites when you need them.
Network
Storage
Ingress
Policies
Plan & apply
Observability
Encrypted network between your sites
Every node runs the network itself. Nodes connect across sites over WireGuard, and routes between them are exchanged with BIRD, so your sites behave like one cluster.
Tunnels only where needed
WireGuard peers exist only between nodes that a policy lets talk to each other.
Addresses that follow
Every service gets a stable IP and DNS name that moves with it when it migrates.
Policy-aware discovery
Cluster DNS only answers for services the caller is allowed to reach.
Shared storage on every node
Volumes are replicated at block level and show up in Docker as a volume plugin. Stateful workloads stay available when a node goes down, from a single node upwards.
Sync nearby, async far away
Synchronous within a site, asynchronous across sites, configurable per volume.
Loss you can see up front
Losing a node loses no data; for losing a site, the plan shows the bounded loss as RPO.
Placement as a policy
For example two synchronous replicas in one site and one asynchronous replica in another.
Ingress that fails over on its own
When the node holding a public IP goes down, the IP moves to a healthy node. Where an IP cannot move, DNS failover takes over. Web traffic and TCP / UDP port forwards are both covered.
Fits your environment
Floating IP on a shared network, BGP announcements, or your provider's failover IP API.
Certificates already there
Built-in ACME; certificates sit on every ingress node, so a failover never waits on issuance.
Limits that hold everywhere
Cluster-wide rate limits, connection limits for port forwards and an optional WAF per hostname.
Everything is a policy
Routing, tunnels, filtering and exposure exist only because a policy allows them. Policies connect groups, like security groups in the cloud, and stay valid when a workload moves to another node.
Deny by default
Nothing talks across groups unless an allow rule says so, and rules are never transitive.
One rule, every layer
An allow rule is compiled into tunnels, routes, firewall rules, the proxy and ingress for you.
Monitor before you enforce
Roll out a policy in monitor mode and see what it would block before it blocks anything.
See every change before it happens
Every change produces a plan: the difference between what you want and what runs, reviewed and then applied. Like Terraform, for your whole cluster.
Failure analysis built in
The plan simulates the loss of every node and site and lists each single point of failure.
Locks that stay out of the way
A plan locks only what it touches, so unrelated changes run in parallel.
Rollback and drift
Failed applies roll back on their own. Changes made outside Loadweaver are reported, never overwritten.
Everything is observable
A live map of every site, node, workload, tunnel and volume, with the traffic between them. Every log the platform produces is one click away.
Live, timeline and plan
Watch traffic live, scrub back through a failover, or overlay a pending plan on the map.
All logs, one query
Containers, proxy, firewall, routing, tunnels and ingress, correlated by deployment, node and policy.
Trace any path
Pick a hostname and see how a request is routed right now, with every policy it passes.
Built around the Docker Compose files you already have
Docker is the base. A deployment is a Compose project, and Loadweaver settings live in extension fields, so the same file still works with plain docker compose.
compose.yaml with Loadweaver extensions (example)
Migration without drama
Every Compose deployment can move between nodes: live where eligible, blue / green where replicas allow, a short stop otherwise. A failed live attempt falls back without data loss.
Pins are explicit
Pinning data, a deployment or traffic to one host is allowed, but the plan warns about it up front. You acknowledge a pin with a reason in the file.
Git if you want it
Everything works in the UI. Connect a repository and pushes create plans, with a plan bot for GitHub and GitLab pull requests.
Runtimes per node
Loadweaver manages the container runtimes on each node, including gVisor next to runc for workloads that need a sandbox.
Capacity kept honest
Every service has CPU and memory requests. The plan warns when the remaining nodes could not take over after a node loss.
Know what breaks before anything breaks
No single host failure takes an app down, unless you pin something to that host on purpose. The plan checks this for every deployment before you apply.

It shows the effect per layer, the DNS records it creates, the capacity left after a node loss and every single point of failure with its cause. The same analysis keeps running afterwards and flags the cluster as at risk until redundancy is back.

How Loadweaver works, from the first policy to the next failover

A control plane that plans and a node agent on every server that applies. Everything you change is declarative YAML, every change is a plan, and every connection exists only because a policy allows it.
Start with policies
Request early access

Loadweaver policy graph: groups for the internet, web, api, database and an office, connected by allow policies with ports and an HTTP rule. A flow from web to the database has no policy and therefore no route. A side panel shows how the api to database policy compiles into a WireGuard peer, a route export and a firewall rule.
Groups, and policies between them
Everything else builds on this. Nodes and workloads join groups, and a policy grants one group access to another, the way security groups work in the cloud. No policy, no connection.
Node groups
Decide which nodes share a network, which get tunnels to each other and which routes are exchanged.
Workload groups
Services join by label, independent of the node they run on, so a rule stays valid when a workload migrates.
Selectors
Membership by selector, such as site = fra1, role = ingress or runtime = sandboxed. Rights add up across all groups.
Built-in groups
internet, cluster, control-plane and one group per site. Platform traffic is a built-in policy too, so it cannot be broken by accident.
One policy, one edge on the map (example)
Enforcing
The control plane compiles each allow rule into every layer it affects
Tunneling
WireGuard peers only exist between nodes that need to talk, with AllowedIPs limited accordingly.
Routing
BIRD only exchanges the prefixes of groups that are allowed to talk.
Filtering
Stateful nftables rules on each node, so return traffic is allowed automatically.
Proxy (L7)
Hostname, URL and SNI rules in Envoy, with mTLS between the node proxies and deny wins inside L7.
Exposure
Ingress and port forwards: "internet" is a group, and exposing a service is an allow from it.
What happens when you change something
The same steps apply whether you click in the console, run the CLI, call the API or push to Git. The control plane is the source of truth; all of them create plans against it.
Describe what you want
YAML, the same language as Docker Compose, with a JSON Schema for editor validation. The UI writes the same YAML.
Get a plan
The difference between desired and actual state, with the compiled effect per layer and every DNS record it creates.
Read the failure analysis
Every single point of failure is listed with its cause, plus the capacity left after losing a node.
Lock only what changes
A plan locks the deployments, groups, policies or nodes its diff touches. Unrelated plans run in parallel.
Apply, or roll back
Failed or cancelled applies roll back on their own. If a rollback fails, you see the real state and a proposed fix-forward plan.
Heal or report drift
What the platform owns is healed automatically. Changes made outside Loadweaver become a proposed plan, never silently overwritten.
No single host failure takes an app down
For every deployment, the plan simulates the loss of each single node and each site and checks whether data, deployment and traffic survive.
The failure domain is the node by default. Surviving the loss of a whole site is an opt-in per deployment or cluster, available from three sites, and validated by the same analysis.
The analysis keeps running after the apply: when a replica is lost or a node degrades, the cluster shows as at risk on the map and in notifications until redundancy is restored.
Pinning is allowed, and visible
You may tie something to one host on purpose. The plan warns about it up front, and you acknowledge it with a reason in the config.
Data
A volume without replicas, replicas only on one node, or bind mounts to host paths.
Deployment
A placement selector that matches one node, one replica without failover, or device access.
Traffic
A failover IP that only one node may hold, or a policy whose only allowed path runs via one node.
Ingress that fails over on its own
Which nodes may hold a failover IP is a node group. When the holder goes down, the IP moves to a healthy member, using whatever your environment supports.

Ingress failover: node n1 in site fra1 becomes unhealthy and releases the failover IP 203.0.113.10; node n4 in site ams1 takes it over and serves web and port-forward traffic. The IP moves via a floating IP, a BGP announcement, a provider failover IP or, where no IP can move, DNS failover.
DNS failover where an IP cannot move
Modes: failover to ordered backups, healthy multi-value answers, weighted answers and geo or latency steering.
Endpoints are probed from at least two sites; a switch needs a quorum of probes and the control plane, so one isolated site cannot flip records on its own.
Hysteresis against flapping and automatic fail-back after a stable period, or manual fail-back per hostname.
Failover records get a low TTL of 30 seconds by default. The plan shows the expected recovery time and is honest that DNS failover is slower and fuzzier than a floating IP.
DNS under the same plan
Records are desired state: ingress hostnames create their records, and the plan shows the DNS diff per provider.
Cloudflare or bind9 hosted in the cluster, behind one provider interface. Loadweaver only touches records it owns, so existing zones can be adopted safely.
Zones with a primary and secondary providers, and opt-in DNSSEC with automatic key rollovers for hosted zones.
Every switch is an event on the timeline, in the audit log and raises an alert.
Configuration in Git, if you want it
Everything can be done in the UI, and everything that is configuration can also live in Git. UI and Git are two editors of the same YAML.
Two ways to combine them
Git is authoritative and UI edits open a pull request, or bidirectional and Loadweaver commits UI changes back with plan id and author. Conflicts show in the plan.
No secrets in the repo
YAML only holds secret references. SOPS-encrypted files are optional, and plaintext secrets in a push are rejected.
Your Git host
GitHub, GitLab, Gitea / Forgejo and plain Git over SSH or HTTPS, triggered by webhooks or polling, per cluster or per project.
GitHub & GitLab
A plan bot in your pull requests

Opening or pushing to a pull request plans automatically. One sticky comment shows the plan diff, pins and failure analysis warnings, quota and capacity impact, image scan results, drift and locks held by other pull requests. A status check links to the plan on the map.
Comments trigger actions, merging does nothing
Applies run on a comment, once the pull request is mergeable and the approval rules are met.
Touched resources stay locked until the pull request is applied, closed or unlocked.
After a successful apply the bot merges the pull request, so the default branch matches what runs.

The policy model

Remote access: a laptop with good posture, a phone with an outdated OS, an office router and a CI runner connect through one endpoint to two WireGuard gateways at different sites. Each reaches only the internal service its group may use; the phone lands in a restricted group that only reaches the helpdesk.
Users, machines and offices
Every client belongs to groups in the same policy model as your workloads. Policies stay allow-only: a client sees nothing unless a policy allows it.
People
A client is a device that belongs to a user. Identity-provider groups map to client groups, so "sales may reach the CRM on 443" is just a policy.
Machines
CI runners, servers elsewhere and office routers connect as machine clients with their own group membership, enrolled by admins.
Offices
Any WireGuard-capable router or firewall, such as OPNsense, pfSense, MikroTik, Fritz!Box or Linux, announces its office subnets. They become a group; overlapping subnets are rejected in the plan.
One endpoint, short-lived keys, routes from policies
Clients never need to know which gateway they use, keys do not live forever, and every client only gets the routes its policies allow.
Gateways
Gateways without a single point of failure

Nodes in a vpn group act as gateways. Clients get one endpoint hostname that resolves via failover IP, anycast or DNS failover, and a client's key is valid on all gateways. A gateway failure means a short reconnect, not a reconfiguration, and a single gateway shows up as a pin.
Self-service enrollment
In the console, desktop app or CLI. The keypair is generated on the device where possible, so the private key never leaves it.
Keys that expire
For example after 30 days, renewed after a fresh sign-in with MFA, since WireGuard itself has no login.
Instant revocation
A revoked device is gone from all gateways at once, and offboarding a user in Keycloak revokes all their devices.
Split tunnel by default
Only the prefixes and service IPs a client's policies allow are routed, and internal names resolve through the policy-aware cluster DNS.
Full tunnel where needed
Groups that need it send all their traffic through the cluster, past the egress proxy and egress policies.
Device posture as a policy condition
"Finance needs an encrypted disk, an OS patched within 30 days and a low EDR risk" is a condition on a client group.
A device that fails its posture moves into a restricted group instead of being disconnected, for example with only the helpdesk and the wiki in reach, and the user sees why.
Core checks
Disk encryption, OS version and patch level, screen lock, OS firewall and app version, reported at connect and periodically.
MDM
Compliance state from Microsoft Intune, Jamf and Kandji, behind a posture plugin interface.
EDR
Risk level from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, CrowdStrike and SentinelOne.
Device certificates
From your company CA, or from Loadweaver's own CA, issued at enrollment.
alice@laptop, not 10.99.0.17
Every client IP maps to a user and a device, so proxy and firewall decisions, logs and the audit trail name the person behind a connection.
On the map
Remote clients appear as a group at the border of the topology map, with live connections and the path trace.
Sessions under control
Admins see active sessions and disconnect or revoke a device instantly. Users see their own devices and last connections.
Alerts
For unusual patterns such as a new country, many denies or posture changes.

Remote access in the console: active sessions named by user and device with their groups, and recent decisions that show alice on her laptop reaching the CRM, bob on his phone being blocked from the CRM by the restricted group but reaching the helpdesk, and the Berlin office reaching the intranet.
